content: 1. Gastrointestinal Disorders: Patients may experience abdominal pain, discomfort, bloating, diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting. 2. General Disorders and Administration Site Conditions: Commonly reported symptoms include fatigue, a general feeling of being unwell, and malaise. 3. Metabolism and Nutrition Disorders: Fluid retention and weight gain have been observed. 4. Musculoskeletal and Connective Tissue Disorders: Muscle spasms and pain in the extremities are possible. 5. Nervous System Disorders: Dizziness, headaches, and drowsiness (somnolence) may occur. 6. Psychiatric Disorders: Insomnia and other sleep disturbances have been reported. 7. Reproductive System and Breast Disorders: Symptoms may include breast pain, breast tenderness, and uterine bleeding. 8. Skin and Subcutaneous Tissue Disorders: Night sweats and itching (pruritus) are potential side effects. 9. Vascular Disorders: Hot flushes are a common vascular symptom. 10. Undiagnosed Abnormal Genital Bleeding: Any unexplained genital bleeding should be evaluated before initiating therapy. 11. Breast Cancer: Therapy is contraindicated in women with known, suspected, or a history of breast cancer. 12. Estrogen-Dependent Neoplasia: Therapy is contraindicated in women with known or suspected estrogen-dependent tumors. 13. Thromboembolic Disorders: Active deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism (PE), or a history of these conditions are contraindications. Similarly, active arterial thromboembolic disease (e.g., stroke, myocardial infarction) or a history of these conditions precludes therapy. 14. Hypersensitivity Reactions: Known anaphylactic reactions, angioedema, or hypersensitivity to estradiol, progesterone, or any excipients are contraindications. 15. Liver Impairment: Therapy is contraindicated in women with known liver disease or impairment. 16. Thrombophilic Disorders: Known deficiencies in protein C, protein S, or antithrombin, or other thrombophilic disorders, are contraindications. 17. Increased Risk of Thromboembolism: Estrogen plus progestin hormone replacement therapy (HRT) is associated with an increased risk of PE, DVT, stroke, and myocardial infarction (MI). 18. Ovarian Cancer Risk: A small but nonsignificant increase in ovarian cancer risk has been reported in studies involving estrogen plus progestin therapy. 19. Dementia Risk: Women aged 65–79 years taking estrogen plus progestin or estrogen alone may have an increased risk of probable dementia. 20. Gallbladder Disease: Postmenopausal women receiving estrogens have a 2to 4-fold increased risk of gallbladder disease requiring surgery. 21. Hypercalcemia in Breast Cancer: Estrogen therapy may cause severe hypercalcemia in women with breast cancer and bone metastases. Therapy should be discontinued if hypercalcemia occurs, and appropriate measures should be taken to reduce serum calcium levels. 22. Retinal Vascular Thrombosis: Women receiving estrogens may experience retinal vascular thrombosis. Therapy should be discontinued immediately if there is sudden partial or complete loss of vision, proptosis, diplopia, or migraine. Permanent discontinuation is warranted if examination reveals papilledema or retinal vascular lesions. 23. Endometrial Hyperplasia: Adding progestin for at least 10 days of an estrogen administration cycle, or daily with continuous estrogen regimens, reduces the incidence of endometrial hyperplasia compared to estrogen alone. Endometrial hyperplasia may be a precursor to endometrial cancer. 24. Blood Pressure Effects: Substantial increases in blood pressure have been attributed to idiosyncratic reactions to estrogens in a small number of cases. However, large clinical trials have not shown a generalized effect of estrogens on blood pressure. 25. Hypertriglyceridemia: Women with preexisting hypertriglyceridemia may experience elevated plasma triglycerides leading to pancreatitis during estrogen therapy. 26. Breast Cancer Risk: Observational studies have reported an increased risk of breast cancer with estrogen plus progestin therapy and a smaller increase in risk with estrogen-alone therapy after several years of use. Risks may persist for over 10 years after discontinuation. 27. Liver Function: Estrogens may be poorly metabolized in women with hepatic impairment. Caution is advised in women with a history of cholestatic jaundice associated with past estrogen use or pregnancy. Therapy should be discontinued if cholestatic jaundice recurs. 28. Thyroid Hormone Replacement: Estrogen administration increases thyroid-binding globulin levels, potentially requiring an increased dose of thyroid hormone replacement in dependent women. 29. Fluid Retention: Estrogens and progestins can cause fluid retention. Caution is advised in women with conditions that may be affected, such as cardiac or renal dysfunction. Therapy should be discontinued if medically concerning fluid retention occurs. 30. Hypocalcemia: Estrogen-induced hypocalcemia may occur in women with hypoparathyroidism. The risks and benefits of therapy should be carefully considered in such cases. 31. Endometrial Implants: Residual endometrial implants have been reported in women treated with estrogen-alone therapy post-hysterectomy. Adding progesterone may be considered for these women. 32. Angioedema: Exogenous estrogens may exacerbate symptoms of angioedema in women with hereditary angioedema. Risks and benefits should be carefully weighed. 33. Exacerbation of Preexisting Conditions: Estrogen therapy may worsen asthma, diabetes mellitus, epilepsy, migraine, porphyria, systemic lupus erythematosus, and hepatic hemangiomas. Risks and benefits should be evaluated in women with these conditions. 34. FSH and Estradiol Levels: Serum follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and estradiol levels are not useful in managing moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms. 35. Arterial and Venous Risk Factors: Risk factors for arterial vascular disease (e.g., hypertension, diabetes, tobacco use, hypercholesterolemia, obesity) and venous thromboembolism (e.g., personal or family history of VTE, obesity, systemic lupus erythematosus) should be managed appropriately. 36. Stroke Risk: An increased risk of stroke has been demonstrated after the first year of therapy and persists. Therapy should be discontinued immediately if a stroke occurs or is suspected. 37. Venous Thromboembolism (VTE): VTE risk increases during the first year of therapy and persists. Therapy should be discontinued immediately if VTE occurs or is suspected. Estrogens should be discontinued 4–6 weeks before surgery associated with increased thromboembolism risk or during prolonged immobilization. 38. Breast Cancer Monitoring: Women should receive yearly breast examinations by a healthcare provider and perform monthly breast self-examinations. Mammography should be scheduled based on age, risk factors, and prior results. 39. Pregnancy and Lactation: Estrogens are not indicated for premenopausal, pregnant, or lactating women. Estrogens and progestins are present in human milk and may reduce milk production. The benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for therapy and potential adverse effects on the child. 40. Food Effects on Absorption: Food increases progesterone absorption (AUC and Cmax) but does not affect estradiol AUC. Food decreases estradiol Cmax and delays peak plasma time to 12 hours. 41. Dosing Instructions: Take each dose in the evening with food. If a dose is missed, take it as soon as possible with food unless it is within 2 hours of the next evening dose. 42. Storage: Store at 20–25°C (68–77°F), with excursions permitted to 15–30°C (59–86°F).
